posts.title: Is High Pressing Actually Taking Over Football? Five Seasons of Data From Europe's Top Five Leagues
posts.dek: “Everyone presses now” is one of modern football's most repeated claims. We pulled team and player event data across the Premier League, La Liga, Bundesliga, Serie A and Ligue 1 to actually test it — and the honest answer is more interesting than a straight yes.
posts.lede: Commentators have been saying it for a decade: the modern game presses harder, higher, and more relentlessly than ever, and possession football is on the way out. It's a good story. We wanted to know if it's a true one — not the vibe, the actual numbers, tested for statistical significance rather than eyeballed off a couple of famous teams.

blocks.html: So we built a dataset: team and player-level defensive-pressure event counts, possession shares, and final league standings across all five of Europe's traditional top leagues, covering as many recent seasons as we could reliably get real data for. Then we asked four specific questions — is pressing volume actually rising, has it come at the expense of possession, does it look different for rich clubs than poor ones, and what's the actual role forwards play in it — and let the data answer each one on its own, even where that meant walking back the premise.

blocks.text: An honest limitation, up front

blocks.html: Team-level defensive-pressure event data (the “Pressures” stat behind most of this piece) comes from a public research mirror of a well-known football-stats site, sourced from event-tracking data. That provider changed hands industry-wide in October 2022, and pressure-event counts specifically stopped being published in our source from the 2022/23 season onward under the new provider's different tracking methodology. Rather than splice two incompatible counting methods into one line and pretend it's a clean trend, we've scoped the pressing-specific analysis to the five full seasons where the same counting method applies throughout: 2017/18 through 2021/22, roughly 490 team-seasons across the five leagues. Possession shares and league tables don't have this problem, so those extend one season further, through 2022/23.

blocks.heading: Why we're not just re-scraping past October 2022
blocks.html: The site itself blocks automated access outright, and re-building years of positional/event data from scratch wasn't realistic for this piece. We'd rather publish five clean, honestly-sourced seasons than stretch a shakier one on top and let a data-provider switch masquerade as a tactical trend — that mistake alone would make a fascinating (wrong) headline.

blocks.text: Is the total volume of pressing actually rising?

blocks.html: Short answer: no — if anything, it's gone slightly the other way. Averaged across all five leagues, the number of defensive-pressure events per 90 minutes peaked in 2018/19 and was lower in 2021/22 than it was at the start of our window.

blocks.caption: League-average defensive-pressure events per 90 minutes, all five top leagues pooled, 2017/18–2021/22 (n≈490 team-seasons). 2020/21's dip lines up with the Covid-disrupted, fixture-congested season — but the overall five-season slope is still a statistically significant decline, not just that one year.

blocks.html: Running a straight regression of press events per 90 against season year, pooled across all ~490 team-seasons, gives a slope of −2.5 events/90 per season (r = −0.24, p = 7×10−8) — small in absolute terms, but about as far from statistical noise as this kind of data gets. It isn't one outlier league dragging the average down, either: four of the five leagues show their own significant downward slope on their own.

blocks.caption: Per-league trend in pressure events per 90, in events/90 per season, 2017/18–2021/22. Four of five leagues decline significantly; Ligue 1 is the one league where the five-season slope isn't distinguishable from flat.

blocks.html: If your mental model of “the pressing revolution” is more of it, every year, everywhere — that's the part of the popular story the data doesn't support, at least not in raw event-count terms.

blocks.text: But raw volume is hiding two real, and more interesting, trends

blocks.html: Total volume falling doesn't mean nothing changed. Two things move in the opposite direction, and both are statistically real:

items: Pressing is getting more efficient. The share of pressure events that actually win the ball back rose from 28.6% in 2017/18 to 29.9% in 2021/22 (slope +0.53 points/season, p = 1×10−13).

What pressing remains is shifting higher up the pitch. The share of a team's pressure events happening in the attacking third — as opposed to their own defensive or middle third — rose from 21.5% to 23.4% over the same five seasons (p = 2×10−7). Attacking-third pressing volume itself is roughly flat (p = 0.09, not quite significant) even while total volume falls, meaning teams are cutting pressing everywhere except up near the opponent's goal.

blocks.caption: Two real five-season trends hiding inside a falling total: pressing has become more concentrated near the opponent's goal, and more likely to actually win the ball, even as the raw event count declines.

blocks.html: Put together, the honest one-line summary isn't “pressing is rising” — it's pressing is getting smarter, not more frequent: less pressing overall, concentrated where it does the most damage, and landing more often when it happens.

blocks.text: Did pressing actually replace possession?

blocks.html: This one needs care, because league-average possession is mechanically stuck near 50% — it's zero-sum within any match, so an aggregate “did average possession fall over time” test is meaningless by construction (and, confirming that, our five-league average sits at 50.0–50.1% every single season). The real question is a cross-sectional one: within a season, do the teams that press more tend to be the teams with less of the ball?

blocks.caption: Every team-season in the dataset: possession share vs. pressing volume (n = 490, all 5 leagues, 2017/18–2021/22). Correlation r = −0.39, p = 5×10<sup>−19</sup> — real, but far from a tight line, which is itself the point: plenty of teams with modest possession press relatively little, and vice versa. Hover a point for the club and season.

blocks.html: That relationship is real and fairly strong: r = −0.39 (p = 5×10−19). Teams with less of the ball do press more — which is exactly what you'd expect mechanically (you can only press when you don't have the ball, so less possession simply means more time available to do it), as much as it reflects a deliberate tactical choice. Where it gets more interesting is asking which style actually works.

series.label: Correlation: pressing volume ↔ points per game

blocks.caption: How strongly each style metric correlates with points per game, season by season. Possession's link to winning has stayed strongly positive throughout (all p < 10⁻¹³); pressing volume's link has stayed negative and, if anything, gotten more so by 2021/22 (p = 1×10⁻⁸).

blocks.html: So: no, pressing hasn't replaced possession as the winning recipe — quite the opposite, on this data. Teams that keep the ball more still win more, consistently, every one of the five seasons we tested. Teams with high total pressing volume tend to have fewer points, not more, and that gap has widened rather than closed. That sounds like it contradicts the “elite pressing team” image (Liverpool under Klopp, Manchester City's own counter-press) — until you separate where the pressing happens, which is the next section.

blocks.text: Rich clubs, poor clubs, and where pressing actually happens on the pitch

blocks.html: We split teams two ways — by final league position (top/middle/bottom third of the table, all five leagues, all five seasons) and, for the Premier League specifically, by total squad market value (bottom/middle/top third by transfer-market valuation, using Transfermarkt data hand-matched to club names). Both cuts tell the same story, independently.

blocks.caption: Where pressure events happen on the pitch, by final-table tercile (all 5 leagues, 2017/18–2021/22). A zone-based proxy for a pitch heatmap — we have defensive/middle/attacking-third counts, not raw x/y coordinates, so this shows the pitch-third split rather than a true positional heatmap.

blocks.html: Bottom-third teams actually generate more total pressure events than top-third teams (156 vs 147 per 90) — but nearly all of that extra volume sits in their own defensive third (55 vs 45 per 90). Top-third teams press less overall, but more of what they do happens in the attacking third (36 vs 32 per 90). In plain terms: for a struggling side, most of what shows up in the stats as “pressing” is really just defending under siege deep in their own half — not the front-foot, opponent's-box gegenpress associated with the elite sides.

The Premier League squad-value cut lands in exactly the same place, independently sourced: teams in the bottom third by squad market value (average €186m) pressed more overall (157 events/90) than the top third (average €804m, 144 events/90), had far less of the ball (44.7% vs 58.0% possession), and pressed less in the attacking third specifically (33.0 vs 35.6 events/90). Across the whole sample, squad value correlates strongly with possession (r = 0.79, p = 5×10−22), negatively with total pressing (r = −0.43, p = 8×10−6), and positively with attacking-third pressing specifically (r = +0.25, p = 0.01).

blocks.heading: “High pressing” is really two different things
blocks.html: Football media uses one phrase for two different behaviors that show up almost as opposites in the data: a rich, dominant side stepping up and squeezing you high in the attacking third, and a struggling side dropping deep and defending for their lives in their own third. Both generate “pressure events.” Only one of them is what people usually mean when they say a team “presses.”

blocks.text: Forwards' role in the press — and how it's shifted

blocks.html: Forwards do the most attacking-third pressing of any position group by a wide margin — unsurprising, since it's the zone they already occupy — averaging 6.1–6.6 attacking-third pressure events per 90 across the five seasons, versus 1.6–1.9 for everyone else combined (defenders, midfielders and goalkeepers pooled, most of whom rarely operate that high up the pitch by design). The more interesting question isn't the gap — it's how forwards' share of that team-wide effort has moved.

series.label: Forwards' share of team's attacking-third pressing

blocks.caption: What share of a team's total attacking-third pressure events came from players listed at forward, by season. Down from 64% to 59% — a statistically significant decline (p = 3×10⁻⁶).

blocks.html: Forwards went from generating roughly two-thirds of their team's high pressing to a little under three-fifths of it (p = 3×10<sup>−6</sup>) — not because forwards are pressing less individually (their own per-90 rate is statistically flat across the five seasons, p = 0.53), but because everyone else's is rising: non-forwards' attacking-third pressing rate climbed significantly over the same window (p < 0.001). The high press hasn't become a forwards' job that's intensified — it's become a whole-team structural job that midfielders and even defenders are being asked to share in more than they used to.

blocks.text: How the top five leagues compare

blocks.caption: Average defensive-pressure events per 90, 2021/22 (the last season our source has a like-for-like count for). The Bundesliga's press-heavy reputation — the Klopp/Nagelsmann/RB Leipzig lineage — holds up as the real top-line number, with La Liga's more patient, possession-first tradition sitting at the other end.

Pitch-zone share of each league's pressing, 2021/22 — the same zone-proxy heatmap as above, split by league. The Premier League and Bundesliga send the largest share of their pressing into the attacking third (≈23.9% each); La Liga sends the least (22.5%) and defends the most in its own third instead.

blocks.text: What this data can't tell us

items: Event-count pressing stats (how many times a player closes down an opponent) are a real signal, but they're a coarser tool than a true positional-tracking metric like PPDA (passes-per-defensive-action) or genuine x/y heatmaps — neither of which we could reliably access for this piece. What's here measures how often teams press and roughly where, not the full coordination and intensity a coaching staff would look at.

The squad-value “rich vs poor” cut is Premier League-only — name-matching Transfermarkt valuations to the other four leagues' club names by hand wasn't practical for this cycle, though the table-position cut (which covers all five leagues) points the same direction independently.

This is a research post, not a model change — nothing here feeds PitchMetric's actual predictions today. If a reliable, current cross-league pressing feed becomes available, a team's pressing profile is a plausible future input to how we think about defensive difficulty; that's not built, and this post isn't claiming it is.

blocks.html: The honest summary: “pressing is taking over” is a catchier headline than what the last five full seasons of data actually show. Total pressing volume is flat-to-down, not up. Possession still predicts winning better than pressing does, and that gap hasn't closed. What has genuinely changed is more specific and more interesting than the popular version — pressing has gotten more efficient, concentrated closer to the opponent's goal, and spread out across more of the team rather than resting on the forwards alone. See Methodology for how PitchMetric's actual predictions work, and the rest of the blog for our other research posts.

posts.tldr: We tested the “football presses harder every year now” claim with real event data across the top 5 European leagues, 2017/18–2021/22. Total pressing volume is actually flat-to-declining, not rising — but pressing has become more efficient and more concentrated in the attacking third, and “high pressing” turns out to mean very different things for rich teams versus poor ones.
keyTakeaways: Pressure events per 90 minutes fell significantly over five seasons (p=7×10⁻⁸), the opposite of the popular narrative — four of five leagues show their own significant decline.
Press success rate and the share of pressing happening in the attacking third both rose significantly — pressing got smarter, not more frequent.
Possession still predicts league points far more strongly than pressing volume does, and that gap widened over the five seasons, not closed.
Rich, table-topping teams press less overall but higher up the pitch; poor teams press more overall but mostly deep in their own third — two different things both get called “high pressing.”
Forwards' share of a team's attacking-third pressing fell from 64% to 59% — the high press has become a whole-team job, not a forwards-only one.

posts.title: Extending the Pressing Study: Three More Seasons, Real Style Clusters, and a Correlation Heatmap
posts.dek: Readers asked two fair follow-up questions on our pressing piece: is there more recent data, and can we bring in heavier tools like clustering and a proper heatmap? Both answers turned out more interesting than a simple yes.
posts.lede: Two good questions landed after our first pressing post: is there more recent data than 2021/22, and could we use more sophisticated methods — clustering to find real attacking styles, a heatmap-style matrix analysis? We went looking for both. One led somewhere useful. The other led to a dead end worth reporting honestly rather than quietly dropping.

blocks.text: The recency question, and a proxy that didn't survive its own test

blocks.html: We found a continuously-updated version of the same public dataset behind our first post, extending team and player stats from 2021/22 through 2024/25 — three more full seasons. Good news for possession, passing, and shot-creation data, which all extend cleanly. Bad news for the specific metric the first post was built on: the raw defensive-pressure event count (“Pressures”) is still completely absent from every season since October 2022, even in this fresher pull. That's not a stale-mirror artifact — it's confirmed again, independently: the current data provider genuinely doesn't publish that stat.

So we tried to build a substitute: a simplified, whole-pitch PPDA-style proxy (opponent passes completed, divided by a team's own tackles + interceptions) computed from stats that do still exist post-2022. Before trusting it for anything, we tested it the only way that matters — does it actually agree with the real, StatsBomb-era press-event numbers on the five seasons where we have both? It doesn't: r = −0.07 (p = 0.11), not distinguishable from zero. A proxy that fails to reproduce the thing it's supposed to approximate, on data where we can actually check, isn't a substitute — it's noise wearing a pressing-shaped costume.

blocks.heading: A negative result is still a result
blocks.html: Real pressing intensity is about where on the pitch defensive actions happen, not just how many there are league-wide. A whole-pitch, unzoned proxy throws that away, and apparently throws away the signal along with it. We're reporting that it failed rather than publishing a number dressed up in confident-sounding language — the same reason we walked back momentum in an earlier piece once it didn't survive testing.

Net result: the specific “is pressing volume rising” trend from the first post still honestly ends at 2021/22. We're not able to responsibly extend it with what's publicly available to us right now. What we can do with the extra three seasons is broaden the question — style, not just volume.

blocks.text: Mapping attack style with real clustering, not vibes

blocks.html: This is the more sophisticated method we hadn't tried yet: unsupervised clustering (k-means) on 96 teams' 2024/25 season, across 18 standardized features — possession, progressive passing and carrying, directness (long-pass accuracy, crossing, through-balls), and the mix of how teams create shots (open-play combination vs. individual dribbling vs. crosses vs. set pieces). No labels, no assumptions about “possession teams” or “counter-attacking teams” going in — we let the numbers group themselves.

We tested cluster counts from 3 to 6 using silhouette score (a standard measure of how cleanly separated clusters actually are) and k=3 won — but with a silhouette of only 0.18, which is modest. Worth being upfront about what that means: these aren't three sharply walled-off tactical tribes, they blend into each other more than they separate. What actually emerged is closer to one dominant spectrum than three distinct styles.

items: Elite tier (13 teams, 62.0% avg possession): Barcelona, Bayern Munich, Real Madrid, Manchester City, Liverpool, Paris S-G, Inter, Atalanta, Leverkusen, Milan, Lille, Tottenham, Brighton. Nobody told the algorithm these were the continent's Champions League regulars — it found that grouping purely from passing, carrying and shot-creation numbers.
Mid tier (39 teams, 53.2% avg possession): Arsenal, Chelsea, Dortmund, Napoli, Atlético Madrid, Juventus, Manchester Utd, RB Leipzig, Roma, and most other recognizable-but-not-quite-elite sides.
Lower-possession tier (44 teams, 43.6% avg possession): the rest — mostly mid-table and relegation-zone sides across all five leagues.

blocks.html: The honest reading: this clustering mostly recovered one axis — call it resource, quality, or dominance — rather than genuinely distinct attacking philosophies. Possession runs 43.6% → 53.2% → 62.0% in a straight progression across the three groups, and so does almost every other feature. That's a real finding, just not the one “style clustering” implies at first glance.

A second dimension does isolate something more like genuine style, independent of quality. Principal component analysis on the same 18 features finds a first axis explaining 46% of the variance — that's the quality spectrum above — and a second, smaller axis (12%) that splits teams by how they create chances: heavy crossing and switches of play at one pole, through-balls and box-entry carries at the other. Crucially, elite teams sit on both ends: Manchester City and Bayern Munich anchor the through-ball/carrying pole, while Inter Milan — built around wing-back crossing — sits at the opposite, crossing-heavy pole, alongside sides like Stuttgart and Mallorca. Being elite doesn't mean playing the same way.

blocks.xLabel: PC1 — overall attacking dominance (46% of variance)
blocks.caption: All 96 teams, 2024/25 season, projected onto the two main axes of attacking style. Left→right is mostly quality/dominance; top→bottom is a real style choice — crossing and switches of play (top) vs. through-balls and carries into the box (bottom) — that cuts across quality levels. Hover a point for the club.

blocks.text: A correlation heatmap across style and results

blocks.html: The other tool worth bringing in properly: a real correlation matrix, rendered as a heatmap, across nine metrics — possession, progressive passing, progressive carrying, crossing, through-balls, passes into the box, long-pass accuracy, shot-creating actions, and points per game — pooled across all five leagues, 2017/18 through 2024/25 (898 team-seasons). Worth being precise about the word “heatmap” here: this is a statistical correlation grid, not a pitch-position heatmap — we still don't have raw x/y event coordinates for that.

blocks.caption: Pearson correlation between each pair of metrics, 898 team-seasons across the top 5 leagues, 2017/18–2024/25. Darker green = stronger positive correlation, darker red = negative. Hover a cell for the exact value.

blocks.html: The matrix mostly confirms the clustering finding from a different angle: progressive passing, progressive carrying, passes into the box, shot-creating actions, and even long-pass accuracy are all tightly inter-correlated (0.6–0.9 with each other, and 0.6–0.67 with points per game) — which means they're mostly measuring the same underlying thing, not five independent skills. One metric stands apart: crossing frequency correlates with almost nothing — barely with possession (r=0.17), barely with points per game (r=0.10), and it's the only pair in the whole matrix with a negative sign at all (r=−0.11 against through-balls). Crossing a lot doesn't mark a team as good or bad — it's a genuinely independent stylistic choice, the closest thing in this data to a real tactical decision uncorrelated with quality.

blocks.text: What this still can't tell us

items: The clustering used a single season (2024/25) as a clean snapshot. Whether a team's style cluster is stable year to year — or shifts with a new manager or transfer window — is a natural next test we haven't run.

k=3 with a silhouette score of 0.18 is a soft, blended grouping, not sharply distinct tactical tribes. Read cluster membership as “closer to this group than the others,” not as a fixed footballing identity.

We still don't have a working substitute for real pressing-intensity data past 2021/22. Our attempt failed its own validation test, and we're leaving that gap open rather than papering over it with a fancier method.

Correlation isn't causation. Teams probably don't win because they complete more progressive passes — both quality and style plausibly share a common cause (squad talent, budget, coaching) that this matrix can't separate out.

blocks.html: See our first pressing post for the full pressing-volume analysis this one extends, and Methodology for how PitchMetric's actual predictions work — none of the clustering or correlation work here feeds the live model today.

posts.tldr: Following up on reader questions: yes, more recent data exists (through 2024/25), but the core pressing-event stat is confirmed gone for good post-2022 — our attempt to build a substitute failed its own validation test. What we could add instead: real k-means clustering of 96 teams' attacking styles, and a genuine correlation heatmap across nine style metrics and results.
keyTakeaways: A PPDA-style proxy built to extend the pressing trend past 2021/22 failed validation against the real metric (r=−0.07, p=0.11) — reported as a negative result rather than shipped.

Unsupervised clustering on 18 style features mostly recovered one quality/dominance spectrum, not sharp tactical tribes — the elite cluster it found unprompted matches Europe's actual superclubs almost exactly.

A second, independent style axis did emerge: crossing/switching-heavy play (Inter, Stuttgart) versus through-ball/carrying combination play (Man City, Bayern) — quality and style aren't the same dimension.

Across 898 team-seasons, most “sophisticated” attacking metrics are so tightly inter-correlated they're really one factor in disguise — except crossing frequency, which correlates with almost nothing, including winning.

posts.title: Has Crossing Actually Gotten More Popular? Testing the Wide-Overlap Narrative With Real Data
posts.dek: Overlapping fullbacks, inverted wingers, whipped-in crosses from the byline — wide play gets talked about as football's growth area. We pulled eight seasons of real passing and touch data across the top 5 leagues to check, and caught a data bug along the way that would have quietly wrecked the answer.
posts.tldr: Crossing volume has not risen — it's declined significantly across the top 5 leagues since 2017/18, and both fullbacks and wingers are recording fewer progressive carries and crosses per 90 than they were seven years ago. We also found no real team-level relationship between how much a team's fullbacks cross and how much its wingers cross, which undercuts the specific “overlapping partnership” story.
keyTakeaways: Team crossing volume fell significantly from 2017/18 to 2024/25 (p<0.001) — the most recent three seasons average meaningfully lower than the first three.
Fullbacks' progressive carries per 90 fell from 2.31 to 2.04 (p<0.001), and their crossing volume fell too — the opposite of a growing overlap trend.
Wingers show the same decline in progressive carrying and crossing over the same window, with a partial late recovery in 2023/24.
A zone-based touch profile confirms the expected pitch hierarchy by role (centre-backs deepest, wingers most advanced) but shows no shift toward wider or more advanced zones over time.

Across 589 team-seasons, a team's fullback crossing volume doesn't correlate with its winger crossing volume (r=−0.03, not significant) — no sign of a real “fullback overlaps, winger cuts inside” structural signature in the aggregate numbers.
We caught a real data-quality issue in the newest season before publishing — see the callout below.
posts.lede: “Fullbacks bomb forward, wingers tuck inside, crosses rain into the box” is a specific, testable claim about how the modern game has changed. We had the data to actually check it: passing types, progressive carries, and touch zones for every player in the top 5 leagues, cross-referenced against Transfermarkt's own position labels (which, unlike the raw stats site, distinguish a left-back from a right winger) so we could isolate fullbacks and wingers specifically rather than lumping every defender and attacker together.

blocks.text: Team crossing volume: down, not up

blocks.html: Across all five leagues, crosses attempted per 90 minutes fell from 18.6 in 2017/18 to 17.5 in 2024/25 — a small-looking number that's nonetheless a real, statistically significant decline (slope = −0.17 crosses/90 per season, p = 7×10<sup>−5</sup>, n = 780 team-seasons). Comparing the first three seasons directly against the most recent three makes it concrete: 18.50 crosses/90 then, 17.53 now (p = 4×10<sup>−5</sup>).

blocks.caption: League-average crosses attempted per 90, all five top leagues pooled, 2017/18–2024/25 (n=780 team-seasons). Three of five leagues (Ligue 1, Premier League, Serie A) show their own significant decline individually; Bundesliga and La Liga are flat.

blocks.html: Crosses specifically aimed into the penalty area (the more dangerous, creative subset) show no significant trend either way (p = 0.56) — so it's not that teams are crossing less overall but aiming better. Total crossing volume is simply down.

blocks.heading: A data problem we caught before publishing
blocks.html: Our first pass at the fullback/winger numbers below showed an alarming result: a sudden ~4x jump in crosses-into-the-box per 90 for both positions in the most recent season, and a positive fullback–winger correlation that vanished the moment we investigated. Digging in, the newest season's player rows paired very small minutes-played totals (as low as 5–8 matches' worth) with counting stats that looked like they belonged to players with 3–4x that playing time — a mismatch between how far along two different stat tables were when our source's snapshot was taken, not a real football signal. We raised our minutes threshold from 450 to 900 minutes (10 full matches) for the player-level analysis below, which fully resolved it — and which meant dropping the newest season (2024/25) from the fullback/winger breakdown entirely, since almost nothing survived that bar there. The team-level crossing trend above doesn't have this problem and keeps all eight seasons.

blocks.text: Fullbacks: progressing and crossing less, not more

blocks.html: Isolating fullbacks specifically (Transfermarkt's Left-Back/Right-Back tags, matched to FBref's per-player stats by player ID, 2017/18–2023/24 after the data-quality fix above): progressive carries per 90 fell from 2.31 to 2.04 (slope = −0.058/season, p < 0.001), and crossing volume fell alongside it (slope = −0.056/season, p = 0.004). Comparing 2018–20 against 2022–24 directly: progressive carries down from 2.36 to 2.10 (p = 8×10<sup>−8</sup>).

blocks.caption: Progressive carries per 90 for fullbacks and wingers (Transfermarkt position tags matched to FBref per-player stats, min. 900 minutes played, 2017/18–2023/24). Both positions decline significantly over the window, with wingers partially recovering in the final season shown.

blocks.html: Wingers show an almost identical shape: progressive carries down from 3.76 to 3.28 across the same first-three-vs-last-three comparison (p = 9×10<sup>−7</sup>), crossing volume down too (p = 0.05, right at the edge of significance). If a wide-overlap revolution were genuinely intensifying, both of these lines should point up. They point down.

blocks.text: Where each position actually touches the ball

blocks.html: A genuine pitch heatmap needs raw x/y event coordinates we don't have access to — same limitation as our pressing research. What we do have is each position's share of touches by pitch third, which gives an honest zone-based proxy for how advanced each role's average position really is.

blocks.caption: Share of touches by pitch third, 2023/24 (the most recent season with reliable player-level data — see the callout above). The hierarchy is exactly what you'd expect — winger most advanced, centre-back least — and fullbacks sit roughly a quarter of their touches into the attacking third, a meaningful step up from centre-backs but well short of a true wide attacker.

blocks.text: Is there a real fullback–winger “overlap” signature in the numbers?

blocks.html: The classic wide-overlap picture has a fullback and a winger on the same flank both contributing to crossing — one underlapping or overlapping the other. If that's a real, common structural choice, teams whose fullbacks cross a lot should tend to also have wingers who cross a lot (both committed to the same wide-combination approach), or possibly the reverse (one crosses instead of the other, trading off). We tested it directly: for each team-season, average fullback crossing volume against average winger crossing volume.

blocks.caption: 589 team-seasons, 2017/18–2023/24. Correlation r = −0.03 (p = 0.50) — not distinguishable from zero. A team's fullbacks crossing more says essentially nothing about how much its wingers cross.

blocks.html: There isn't one. Not a positive relationship (both committing to crossing together) and not a clean negative one (one deputizing for the other) — just noise. Whatever specific tactical relationship exists between a fullback and winger on the same flank, it isn't showing up as a simple volume correlation in season-aggregated stats. That doesn't rule out real coordinated overlapping within matches — it just means this particular aggregate signature isn't evidence for or against it, and we'd need event-level, same-possession data to actually test the real claim.

blocks.text: What this data can't tell us

items: Touch-share by pitch third is a zone-based proxy, not a true positional heatmap — we still don't have raw x/y event coordinates for that, same limitation as our pressing research.

Transfermarkt's position tags reflect a squad's listed/primary role, not which flank a player played on in any specific match — a right-footed “Left-Back” who mostly plays inverted, or a squad's rotation between roles mid-season, isn't captured.

“Overlap” as coaches use it is a same-possession, ball-near event (a specific run timed against a specific teammate's touch) — season-aggregate crossing totals can't directly test that; the correlation test above is a reasonable but indirect proxy.

The newest season (2024/25) is missing from the fullback/winger breakdown after we caught the minutes/stats mismatch described above — we'd rather publish seven clean seasons than eight with one silently wrong.

posts.title: Inside a 3-3 Classic: Mapping Spain vs Portugal's Passing Network With Real Event Data
posts.dek: Everything on this blog so far has run on season-aggregate stats. Passing networks and graph theory need something different — real pass-by-pass event data with pitch coordinates. We found a legitimate free source for it and rebuilt one of football analytics' classic visualizations from scratch.
posts.tldr: We sourced real match event data (StatsBomb's open-data project) to build genuine passing networks — not season aggregates — for Portugal 3-3 Spain at the 2018 World Cup, then applied real graph-theory metrics (degree, betweenness, eigenvector centrality) to find each team's structurally important players. We also built a pass-by-pass sequence map for one of the six goals. This is a capability demonstration on a specific open dataset, not (yet) something feeding this week's Premier League predictions.
keyTakeaways: Passing networks need event-level data (who passed to whom, and from where) — a different, harder-to-get data tier than the season totals every other post on this blog has used.

StatsBomb's open-data project is a legitimate, free source of that data for a defined set of competitions — several World Cups and Euros, many Champions League seasons, and a large chunk of Barcelona's La Liga history — though it doesn't cover most current-day Premier League or La Liga fixtures.

Graph theory adds real information beyond raw pass counts: betweenness centrality found Sergio Ramos and Raphaël Guerreiro as each team's structural “bridge” players, distinct from (and more interesting than) simply who touched the ball most.
Spain's network was denser but less clustered than Portugal's — a real, quantified difference in shape, not just a visual impression.
This is a demonstrated capability on a specific dataset, not a live feature — it doesn't feed PitchMetric's actual predictions today.
posts.lede: Ronaldo scored a stoppage-time free kick to complete his hat-trick and salvage a 3-3 draw against Spain in the opening game of the 2018 World Cup — still one of the most-replayed group-stage matches in tournament history. It's also, conveniently, a match with full public event data available: every pass, carry and shot, with real pitch coordinates, freely published. That makes it a good test case for a capability question worth answering properly rather than faking: can we build the kind of passing-network and graph-theory visualizations serious football analytics accounts publish — with real data, not a mockup?

blocks.text: A different kind of data for a different kind of chart

blocks.html: Every research post on this blog so far — pressing, style clustering, crossing trends — has run on season-aggregate stats: a player's total progressive passes for a whole year, a team's average possession. A passing network needs something categorically different: event-level data, one row per pass, with who played it, who received it, and exactly where on the pitch both of those happened. FBref (our usual source) doesn't publish that. We went looking for a legitimate public source that does, and found one: StatsBomb's open-data project, which freely publishes full event data — coordinates included — for a defined set of competitions: several men's and women's World Cups, the Euros, many Champions League seasons back to the 1970s, and (thanks to a long-running public tracking project) a large chunk of Barcelona's La Liga history.

blocks.heading: Worth being precise about what this covers
blocks.html: This is real data for specific released matches — not a live feed, and not current-day Premier League or La Liga coverage (StatsBomb's PL open release stops at 2015/16). What follows is a genuine demonstration of the technique on real data, not a new capability quietly powering this week's gameweek posts.

blocks.text: 67′ and 69′: Portugal 3–3 Spain, World Cup 2018

blocks.html: Each network below uses every completed pass up to that team's own first substitution (Portugal, 67′; Spain, 69′) — the standard convention, since a substitution changes the team's actual shape and personnel. A player's position on the pitch is their average pass-origin location across that window — not a formation diagram, an emergent one built from where they actually touched the ball. Node size is pass volume; node color is betweenness centrality (more on that below); edge thickness is passes exchanged between that specific pair.

Spain, passes 1–69′. Busquets and Sergio Ramos sit at the center of a visibly denser web — consistent with Spain's reputation for circulating possession through a settled shape.

blocks.text: What graph theory actually adds beyond “who has the most passes”

blocks.html: Treating the network as an actual weighted graph (using NetworkX, the standard Python graph library) unlocks metrics that raw pass counts can't give you. Degree centrality is close to just “how many teammates did you exchange passes with” — useful, but in a possession-heavy match it saturates quickly (several players on both sides touch every one of their ten teammates at least once, so degree centrality maxes out at 1.0 for half the team and stops discriminating). Betweenness centrality is more interesting: it measures how often a player sits on the shortest connecting path between two teammates who don't otherwise link up directly — a structural “bridge” role, not just a busy one.

By betweenness, Portugal's most structurally important player wasn't Ronaldo or Bernardo Silva — it was left-back Raphaël Guerreiro (0.31), the connector between defense and attack down the left. For Spain, it was center-back Sergio Ramos (0.31), reflecting his role building from the back rather than just his passing volume (which was high anyway — he led the whole match). Neither is a surprising name in hindsight, but it's a different, sharper claim than “this player touched the ball a lot,” and it's the kind of thing raw stats tables don't surface on their own.

The two networks also differ in shape by real, computed measures, not just by eye: Spain's network is denser (0.891 vs Portugal's 0.855 — the share of all possible player pairs who actually exchanged a pass) but less clustered (0.176 vs 0.247 — how much a player's teammates also passed to each other, not just to them). Spain circulated the ball through more total connections; Portugal's connections leaned more on tight local triangles around specific players.

blocks.text: One goal, pass by pass

blocks.html: The same event data lets us reconstruct a single passage of play move by move — useful for a specific goal rather than a whole match's shape. Diego Costa's second goal (54:02, making it 3–2 Spain) started with a long diagonal switch from David Silva, cushioned first-time by Sergio Busquets into Costa's path for the finish:

blocks.caption: Diego Costa's goal, 54:02: David Silva → Koke → David Silva (carries the ball infield) → a long diagonal ball to the edge of the box → Busquets lays it off first-time → Costa finishes. Six real events, numbered in order, dashed arrows are carries rather than passes.

blocks.text: What this means for PitchMetric

items: This is a capability demonstration on a specific, freely available dataset — it does not feed PitchMetric's live predictions, and there's no current plan that it will, since we don't have this depth of event data for the current Premier League or La Liga seasons.

“Value” in these networks is pass count, not an expected-threat (xT) weighting per pass location — some published examples layer an xT model on top of the raw counts, which is a real additional modeling step we haven't built.
Betweenness and eigenvector centrality here treat mutual passing as one undirected tie (standard practice for pass networks) — it loses some direction information a directed-graph version would keep.

One match is one match. A single game's network reflects that day's specific tactical plan and scoreline as much as any stable team identity — treat this as an illustration of the method, not a claim about either team's general style.
